utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. It's -- I'll show you the Albanian version, and it's 65 ter 1919. I'd like you to look at paragraph 17 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd just like, if I may, to seek some clarification as to the basis upon which this is being done, because I think Mr. Di Fazio is aware that this witness, when interviewed by the Prosecution in May, indicated certain things about certain passages in his statement, including this one, which makes it somewhat surprising that it's being put to him at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is there any reason why you first draw the attention of the witness to his statement rather than elicit his evidence, if at least if you want to elicit the evidence of paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The witness has said he can't remember. He's provided this statement in the past in which he does provide commentary on this episode, on an episode that occurred there. It may assist in refreshing his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, if the purpose is memory-refreshing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness take his earphones off for a second. Mr. Fazliu, could you take your earphones off for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I also point out that the witness has on the screen in front of him the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put that off. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If the purpose is memory-refreshing, then I'm sure Mr. Di Fazio's own memory will serve us right. This is a passage about which he asked him during a videolinked interview on the 11th of May. Unless I'm much mistaken - I'm looking at the passage now - it was a passage that the witness just found, in which case the purpose isn't memory-refreshing at all unless he's putting both passages to him and asking him which is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, would you put both passages to him in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm more than willing to put both passages to the witness, if Your Honours please. Perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check with the other Defence counsel. Would that be a course to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's one way of approaching it. Another would simply be for Mr. Di Fazio to ask him directly rather than, Did you see one of your relatives? Ask him outright: Did you see Lahi Brahimaj? I have no objection to that and maybe that will get us where we're going much faster and more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, earlier, I think the witness explained that one of the accused was a -- although a relative, quite far away, so that might cause some confusion. I leave it up to you which of the two suggested courses you will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm content with the question that I asked. I don't want to ask any question. I asked him if he saw any relatives. He's provided evidence about his relationship with the accused in this case. He says he can't remember. I'm happy to adopt Mr. Emmerson's suggestion and put both versions to the witness and ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think until now neither of these suggestions has been objected by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There has been no objection, but considering that I think what we're trying to do is understand a specific fact that Mr. Di Fazio is seeking, I would adopt the suggestion that's presently been made by Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I didn't make myself -- if I didn't make myself clear enough, that is also my suggestion. The point I was making was simply Mr. Di Fazio is aware that there are passages in this witness statement that this witness does not accept were correct, and to launch straight in to seeking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are objecting to as a matter of fact is to refresh his memory in only one direction or not the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Or simply to ask the witness what occurred at a particular place is the way forward, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is this sufficient for you, that the main objection is against refreshing his memory on the basis of one specific statement, and a lot of suggestions, I take it that you'll find your way through it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I have a number of suggestions. I'm happy to refresh this witness' memory. He said he can't remember - he said he can't remember - let's be clear about that, on the basis of what Mr. Emmerson wants me to put, namely, what he said to the Prosecution during an interview and also on the basis of the -- of a prior -- another statement made on another occasion. I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise, because this is an untidy way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that, Mr. Di Fazio, he doesn't remember. Perhaps you directly put that question to him, and then, of course, I can understand that you then put to him that he gave different statements on that and then to ask for further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you recall having any conversation with any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have to ask the witness to put his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see any KLA members in Gllogjan on your way to Zabelj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Maybe there were and certainly there must have been because it was a wartime. But I can't give you any names. There were many such people moving up and down, some using vehicles, some walking on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can't recall the names of anyone who you -- any KLA men that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. I saw someone in uniform in Jabllanice, Lahi Brahimaj with a colleague of his whom I don't know. Maybe this is why the mistake is, that is Gllogjan is mentioned. The fact is that we met Lahi Brahimaj on the way to Gllogjan. But this happened in Jabllanice, not in Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who precisely is Lahim?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Lahi Brahimaj, Mr. Lahi Brahimaj, who is here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you meet him in -- sorry, I withdraw that. You can't recall seeing any of your relatives in Gllogjan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: My cousins are in Dasinoc and Turjaka. There weren't any cousins of mine there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was Lahi Brahimaj one of your cousins that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw Lahi in Jabllanice. He was in a car. And he stopped and we talked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: He greeted us. He opened the door of the car. He greeted us. I was with my travelling companion, as you put him -- put it. And he asked us where we were going and we said that we were going in the direction of Zhabel. I was carrying an automatic rifle with me. And he said, "Is it possible that you give me this automatic rifle because there are some soldiers at the front line without weapons," and this is what I did. But I asked him to give it to me when I needed it, which really happened. But on this occasion Naser gave of his own free will two bombs, because he didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that the only conversation you had with Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: At the moment we met him, that was all we exchanged. When I gave him my weapon, we saluted each other. Then they went on their way in their car; we continued to work in the direction of Zhabel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And when you got to Zabelj, what did you -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: We arrived very late; maybe it was 10.00 or 1100. I can't be sure. I didn't have a watch. Naser showed us the way and we went to the house of Tal Zeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you whether it was the evening or the morning, 10 or 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was evening. It was late and I was drenched to the skin because it was raining all day now and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were there numbers of other people taking refuge at this house, other Albanians?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you and your travelling companion remain at this house?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I can't be sure. If I'm not mistaken, some three nights, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And during that period of time were you visited by any KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: One day a group of soldiers came. Nazmi Brahimaj was one of them. We had a conversation at the guestroom of Tal Zeka, in the oda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is Nazmi Brahimaj related to Lahi Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: He was his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What conversation was -- well, let me withdraw that. Were there any other KLA men who came to the house on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I remember there was someone, a commander of Zhabel, I think his name was Tahir, and three or four other soldiers whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the conversation that you had?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: It was mainly Nazmi who did the talking. It was about our return to the villages where we had left from following the attack by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was he addressing his comments to you and your travelling companion or to a wider group of people?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: He was addressing all of us. He meant his words for all the villagers. He was discussing with us how to find the way for them to go back to their home and about the shortage of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And is this villagers from Grabanica or a wider area?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said that Nazmi Brahimaj was addressing you about going back to your villages and the shortage of arms. Were these comments -- were these comments being addressed to villagers from your village, Grabanica, or were they being addressed to a group of people from more than just one village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: All of us who were there in the room, in the oda, he was addressing all of us without making any distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were they all Grabanica villagers, all of you in that oda, or were there other villagers from other villages as well?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, there were two people from Turjaka but I don't know them. Otherwise, six or seven of us, I think, were from Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And presumably all LDK supporters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think I mentioned that even earlier, that until the situation deteriorated, all of us belonged or supported the LDK. After that I can't be sure because people might have changed their beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm looking at the clock. We need a break. Would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is a fine moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness -- Mr. Fazliu, we will have a break, approximately 20 minutes. Madam Usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we return into open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Di Fazio, could you give us an impression of how much more time you'll need? Some time was taken by procedural matters, but I think you informed the Chamber that you would need approximately one hour. If I deduct 10 minutes for procedural matters, we're about at that hour. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I rather expect that the remainder of this witness' testimony will pass fairly swiftly. Can I say I'd need about another 20 minutes. I know that I'm exceeding the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Defence who do not know what is still there to come, could the Defence give an impression on what they expect at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would be very reluctant to commit myself to completing cross-examination today if we're looking at another 20 minutes of examination-in-chief, if that's a sufficient answer for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, perhaps later today I might put the question to you again, closer to 7.00, and to the other counsel as well. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly will have some questions over and beyond Mr. Emmerson. As Your Honours will well appreciate, this matter comes a little closer to home for my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At present I have four questions. I trust it won't be more, many more than that based on the way examinations have gone previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will put the same question to you again closer to 7.00, also because the Chamber needs a bit of time tomorrow for procedural matters as well, and of course we have to finish with this witness before we adjourn tomorrow, not sitting on Friday, not sitting on Monday. We'll take a break of 20 minutes. That means that we'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've -- sorry. You told us that Nazmi Brahimaj addressed you men at the house of -- at the house in Zabelj and asked you to go back to your villages. Did he explain to you what he wanted you to do back in your villages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we returned into open session, so I think in view of what we discussed before the break, unless your line of questioning would not require further reference to the reason why we went into private session --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll be coming back to that particular personality in a while, but for the moment we can go back into open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So please keep in mind to return into private session in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood. Yes, we can remain in private session. Thank you. Thank you for alerting me, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore -- no, now the confusion is complete. Just prior to the break, we returned into open session when I asked questions about timing, so we now resumed in open session; but I do understand, and perhaps that's a wise thing to do, is to return into private session at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said before the break that Nazmi Brahimaj had asked you to go back to your village. Did he explain for what reason, what he wanted you to do?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Nazmi Brahimaj came so that when the conditions were ripe and when we had enough weapons, he wanted to sound out our readiness to see how ready we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. And did he sound out your readiness at the house of -- at the house that you were at in Zabelj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. We -- at least I speak for myself, but it's more difficult to remain in another village than in your own village. So for us it was easier for me to go back to my village. It's easier even to die in your village than in another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was this readiness to fight, to engage in armed conflict against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. We were ready from the 13th onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you about Nazmi Brahimaj. Nazmi Brahimaj, in the house in Zabelj, did he ask you and ascertain from you, you in particular and also the other men who were gathered there with you, your fellow villagers, whether you were ready to fight back in your village? Did he ask you that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: He didn't ask a personal question of any one of us, but it was in general that he spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was the readiness that he was inquiring about, readiness to engage in armed conflict against the Serbs, was that the readiness that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: That was the main aim for all of us, to fight the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It might have been the main aim for all of you. It's a very simple question that I have. Was that what Nazmi Brahimaj was trying to ascertain from you? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to stay a little bit far from the microphone because we hear his breathing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I was just writing a question to Madam Usher to the same effect. Perhaps if we adjust the microphone a little bit so that the witness can be heard well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you or the assembled men indicate anything in response to Nazmi Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I remember that I engaged in a conversation with one of the soldiers whose nickname was Ujku, meaning wolf. I don't know his name. In my opinion he didn't meet the criteria to be a soldier because he spoke in some rather odd expressions. But in times of war maybe people speak even in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Let me approach this topic in another way. Following this discussion or -- this discussion with Nazmi Brahimaj, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, no. That day the conversation lasted more -- not more than five or ten minutes, and then they went to Jabllanice or to some other front place. I don't know. We remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you revisited at that house by KLA men on subsequent days?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the next day Ujku, or wolf, came. It was either I think mid-day or afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he alone?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I think he came with a person called -- I mentioned his name in my statement. At this moment I don't remember his name. He is also from Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which statement would that be?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: In the statement I gave to the -- to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That was an accurate detail that you sought to give on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: His last name is Zeneli. I don't remember. Now I do. Arbnori Zeneli. That is, Ujku came with Arbnor Zeneli.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you gave that detail you were trying to be truthful and give an accurate detail to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Which detail are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About Zeneli.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Arbnor Zeneli. Ujku came with Arbnor on the next day on the talk that we had with Nazmi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. On this occasion when Arbnor and Ujku came, what was the topic of conversation?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, Ujku started the conversation with softer tones, but then later he started using insulting expressions. Initially he said that we should go to Jabllanice to assist in digging the grave of some youth who had committed suicide. Then he changed what he said earlier and his stand and he started to insult us. I wouldn't say the same of Arbnori. He didn't insult us in any way. On the contrary, he criticised Ujku.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you go to -- did you eventually leave the house at which you were staying?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: We left the house and the words we exchanged with them were at the end of the stairs. Tahir, that commander of Zabelj was there, and both Arbnori and Tahir rebuke Ujku for his conduct towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave the house and go to another village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: After this we, together with Naser and two other co-villagers, we continued. Ujku got on a car and he left for somewhere. I never saw him. And together with some soldiers and Tahir, the commander of Zabelj, we continued our way. He asked me about my life, my profession. These are the kinds of conversations we had until Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As clearly as you can, please, explain to the Trial Chamber why you left the house and went to Jablanica in the company of this KLA men? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I already stated that one day earlier we discussed the need to discuss and come up with a unified stand on remobilising ourselves and returning to the previous positions in Jabllanice and in Bokshiq, the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what you discussed the day before. But why did you go to Jablanica in company with these KLA men? Just tell us clearly and expressly why that was so.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said that Ujku raised a concern but Arbnori later explained the situation, telling us that we had to talk about our mobilisation. Why shouldn't we all go together, he said, myself and the other, and discuss what the Serb forces were doing against the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And how many men were --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Di Fazio continues, I'm looking at the transcript at page 73, line 24, where it says "returning to the previous positions in Jabllanice and Bokshiq." I wonder, certainly from listening, whether the witness intended to say Jabllanice or Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This has been clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Apart from the KLA men who went to -- who were accompanying you, how many of you villagers were going in this party towards Jablanica? Just how many men, apart from the KLA men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Myself and my travelling companion, Fadil Selmani and Ali Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All from Grabanica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, no. Yes, yes. The four of us were from Grabanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were -- I withdraw that question. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: You mean to Jabllanice from Zhabel?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: We walked on foot, talking on the way, as if you do in normal situation, with Tahir, and we didn't have any problem. He asked me where I worked. I told him that I was a principal of the school for so and so years. I explained to him my education. Then I asked him what he was doing and he said that he was working in Switzerland. Things like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were all of you -- all of you men from Grabanica content to go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't have a problem with that. I am not a psychologist to know what the others were thinking. But as far as I am concerned, nothing worried me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you anxious to discuss your mobilisation with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the way to there I asked Tahir why he had returned from Switzerland and he said that he came back because he wanted to contribute to the country's liberation. These were the sort of conversations we had with him on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But were you, Mr. Fadil Fazliu, were you anxious to get to Jablanica and discuss your mobilisation with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just slightly concerned about potential ambiguity in the question, particularly through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you, Mr. Fadil Fazliu, keen to go to Jablanica and speak to the KLA about fighting or going back to Grabanica to fight?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I would have preferred at that time to have enough weapons to fight the enemy as we wished, but I didn't have much confidence that, given the weapons we had at our disposal, we would be able to fight such a force, that we had to fight like the paramilitaries and other Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you keen at the time that you were going towards Jablanica to go to Jablanica and discuss fighting or mobilisation with the KLA? That's my question. That's my question. It's not whether or not you had good weaponry. It's not whether you found yourself in an ideal situation. I understand that. My question is simply this: Were you keen at the time to go to Jablanica and discuss the question of mobilisation or fighting in Grabanica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the same kind of objection as with the previous question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word "keen," just as the word "anxious," could be easily mistranslated and have several meanings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What Mr. Di Fazio is trying to get at is whether the witness went voluntarily. If that's the question he's seeking an answer to, then it can be put in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let Mr. Di Fazio reformulate his question and then we'll hear what exactly he wants to find out. But both the word "anxious" and the word "keen" could have several meanings and could easily create confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you want to go to Jablanica and discuss mobilisation and fighting wherever with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Even though we understand your question rather differently, I agree with you that I had a positive reaction to the talk. I understand that you, asking me this question, want to find out whether I was forced to go there, which is not the case. Nobody used any force against me. Nobody pushed me to go there by force. I went there with my own free will. I might have also refused to go there. But I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber if you'd given any thought to going to Jablanica to speak to the KLA about fighting or mobilisation prior to this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I remember it was 1998. I was with someone called Elvir Berisha, a colleague of school. We went with his tractor along Nepol [phoen] river and we went to Jabllanice. We remained there until after midnight and had conversations with some people there who were standing guard duty in Jabllanice, among them was Murt Zeneli. Lahi, I think, wasn't there that night because he was somewhere else on business.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- that's -- thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: So the conversation lasted one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks for that explanation. I appreciate that. But if we could just go back to my question, could you answer it, please. My question is this: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber if you'd given any thought to going to Jablanica to speak to the KLA about fighting or mobilisation prior to you actually going there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He just answered that question, Your Honour. I think that it's a bit confusing in the manner that it's been posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see no answer in that -- in that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question could be put to the witness again. Could you please try to focus on what Mr. Di Fazio asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that the first efforts were made even earlier, but we decided together with Enver Berisha, and we went there and the entire talk we had was focused on the arms supply for villages that were in our locality, in our municipality, Grabanice, Qeskove. Because Enver was from Qeskove. We had this talk with Murt Zeneli and other villagers on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way: On your way to Zabelj, were you considering going to Jablanica to discuss mobilisation or fighting with the KLA during that part of your trip?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber why you didn't go to Jablanica at that point to discuss fighting and mobilisation with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: At which moment are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the way to Zabelj.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: From Zhabel we went to Jablanica headquarter and there we had similar talks as the one we had with Nazmi one day earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, it seems that until -- unless I misunderstood the question, I think the question was why didn't you go directly to Jablanica to discuss these matters rather than first go to Zabelj? I think that's what Mr. Di Fazio is interested to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained earlier. It was night. It was maybe from 9.00 to 11.00 in the evening when we travelled. And the place that my companion wanted to go was far, so we had to go to this place, stay there, rest a while, and that question of mobilisation could wait. It could be discussed on the next day or on the following day, because, as I said, I was wet to the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. That explains part of it. But having woken up the next day and presumably not being wet to the bone, at that point why didn't you go to Jablanica and discuss mobilisation with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I am sorry, but really all my clothes were wet and the family members of Tal, they took them to clean and to dry. So it took some time for all this to be done. So I remained in the room with a T-shirt and with a pair of trousers that they lent me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: These KLA guys, Nazmi and the other man, Ujku, they came over a period of two days to the house there, didn't they? Do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the first day, yes. On the second day it was only Ujku and Arbnori who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make any effort to go to Jablanica and discuss mobilisation on the first day when Nazmi came?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: It was late afternoon when he came, if I'm not mistaken, and I had nothing to prevent me from going there, because even my brother was being treated in Jablanica. He was wounded in fighting in Grabanice and I could hardly wait to go and visit even my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you explain to Nazmi your keenness, or, rather - let me withdraw that, I won't use that word - your desire to, A, see your brother and, B, discuss mobilisation with the KLA, or at least perhaps ask him to help you achieve your objective?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I think that would be no obstacle on the part of Nazmi, and bearing also in mind the family connections because he knew who my brother was and they had tried their best to heal wounds of my brother who was being treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, anyway, it took you two days before you could achieve your desires and make your way to Jablanica to do the various things that you wanted to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that that question mischaracterises the witness' testimony and it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In any event, two days elapsed before you were able to go to Jablanica and achieve whatever it was you wanted to achieve there.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said it earlier. I could not leave the house undressed, and that was because of the conditions. There were no other change of clothes that I could use. And the way I was dressed, I could not even get out of the doorstep of that house. And I was not the only person who had taken shelter in that house and there were other people and they were in a similar situation, they had similar needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, anyway, eventually you did make your way to Jablanica. About what time did you arrive there? And can I also ask you to address your mind to this issue, thinking back: What was the date that you arrived in Jablanica, if you can remember? I don't invite you to speculate. If you're not sure, say so. So I'm asking you two questions in one. When did you get there? And secondly, if you know, what date did you get there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Could have been the 24th but I'm not sure. It was in the afternoon. I did not have a watch on me to know exactly with minutes' accuracy. But it was the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At that time in May of 1998, did you know Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you know Idriz Balaj?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I never knew Idriz. I only saw him first when he appeared in this -- before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you got to Jablanica, you went to the KLA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: We went into the courtyard of the army headquarters in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you stay there in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: We stayed in the courtyard. There were some other people from Bokshiq, and I cannot remember the names of those people. We had a conversation with a man with a moustache, Gani, who had brought food, cheese, and other foodstuff, and people there managed to eat whatever they could. And in the meanwhile we were talking about mobilisation and better preparations to counter the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave Jablanica that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: When all the conversations were over, we concluded that for the moment we could not get enough weapons because the Serb forces were in great numbers and we would have to wait for a more convenient moment to get weapons. And then we went outside the courtyard and Arbnor was waiting in a car that he could take us to wherever we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I gather you got to Jablanica that day, you stayed there for a period of time, and you left Jablanica the same day. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All in all, how long would you say you stayed in Jablanica from the time of your arrival to the time of your departure?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I may just guess because we travelled very slowly from Zhabel to Jablanica. It was like a walk at a picnic pace. So it was probably about two hours and a half. But I cannot say exactly for how long we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So is it correct that it was a matter of hours, no more, that you were actually in Jablanica village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many hours. It was in the afternoon that we left Zhabel, plus the travel time. I cannot be more accurate on how long we stayed there. It took a bit of time until people had something to eat and then some people had tea and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the man described as your travelling companion, was he also present with you when you arrived in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: He was with us all the time. Like the rest of the villagers there, he had things to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what did you, you in particular, Mr. Fazliu, discuss in terms of mobilisation with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: Our conversation, and given the family connections, the main conversations I conducted were with Lahi and Nazmi, and the main conclusion was that there was a -- in the lack of enough weapons, we'll have to wait for a more convenient moment when there were enough weapons, and that not only me but the rest of the people who were there would willingly return to their villages to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where was your weapon at that time, the time that you were in Jablanica discussing this issue?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I gave my weapon to Lahi as -- and that was of my own free will, and I told him that he would return it to me when I needed it, and it so happened when I asked him for that, he did return it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what plans were made -- sorry, Your Honours, I'll just withdraw that. Were any clear plans made for you and your fellow villagers to mobilise? By that I mean were any clear dates set? Were any lists of names drawn up as to who should be mobilised or who should be doing what? Anything that was more concrete beyond a decision to mobilise at some uncertain point in the future?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: No date was set, but where each one of us stood, we -- everything was recorded there at the headquarters. We recorded the names of where people are at that particular -- were at that particular time, although some people had crossed into Montenegro. But there was enough information to mobilise people whenever that moment had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And were any specific plans made beyond future mobilisation in respect of you and Grabanica villagers?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: That was difficult. It was difficult to draw up a specific plan and that is because of the difficult geographic position that Grabanica and Bokshiq have. It's -- that area was endangered by three -- from three directions; from the Serbs in Dollova, on the other side it was the main road 200 metres away, and on the other side there was Drenoc and other villages where there were a large amount of weaponry and forces. And that was why no specific plan could be drawn up to be enacted against the Serbian forces in the circumstances when there was a lack of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So two factors, two factors, militated against anything specific: Lack of weapons and these geographic considerations relating to the positions of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: There was another third factor which had a great significance because the Lugu i Baranit was not included in the war zone and there wasn't a possibility for the Serb forces to come through the village of -- through Lugu i Baranit and straight to our area. So we were waiting for Lugu i Baranit to be included in the war zone before we started to think about the mobilisation of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the light of these factors that really made it difficult to come up with any specific plan, do you know why it was important to get you and your travelling companion and your fellow villagers from Zabelj to Jablanica that very day? Do you know of any other -- do you know of any compelling reason why that should be so?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw no compelling reason in addition to the ones from the positive aspect. It was only to organise a meeting with all those who had been forced to leave their home villages because of the circumstances and to discuss the issues with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that, this discussion concerning mobilisation, did you eventually leave the area of the KLA headquarters and go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, outside the gate of the headquarters, Arbnor was waiting for us in a car and he told us that he would take us, drive us, to wherever we wanted to go. And we were driven to the house of Hadzi Bajrami. That's where we wanted to go and that's where we were taken to. That's where I parted ways with my travel companion. I went to a friend called Maznik, Zylaj, and I stayed there for four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm just about finished. I just want to ask you one or two more questions about numbers. When this mobilisation was being discussed at the KLA headquarters, how many men would you say were assembled, or present at least, to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: As far as the people in uniform are concerned, as I said earlier, I recalled there were five of them. Some of them were -- when the guards were changed, some of them maybe were having something to eat; some were having tea. But as far as we were concerned, we were more than ten people from Grabanice and Bokshiq. In the meantime, Beqir Beqiri arrived. Deliu, Mustafa Deliu, Uk Bardheci, and I can't remember other names. But there were 10, probably 15 people present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were the majority LDK members -- LDK sympathisers?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: This question is being repeated frequently, but I said earlier there was no time to ask which party affiliation people had at that time. The situation did not allow for such questions to be asked..

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you go actually inside the KLA headquarters or did you remain in the yard eating the food that Gani had brought you, and discussing mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: I had some water from the well and then I sat around the table that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the yard or inside the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: FADIL FAZLIU
utterances.text: The well is in the courtyard. That's where I got some -- had some water. And then I entered the canteen where food was served and where the conversations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Emmerson, since I have a few procedural matters, I think it would be better that cross-examination starts tomorrow, because we have only seven minutes left. I would need those seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour asked for a time estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I always prefer to do that in the absence of the witness, since we do not need the witness anymore. Mr. Fazliu, we're close to 7.00, where we always finish. Tomorrow you'll be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have already given today or you are still about to give tomorrow. We'd like to see you back in Courtroom I - that's a different courtroom - tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. I'll ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, one observation about the beginning of this court session. As it is said in Porgy and Bess, it is very difficult to divorce woman that ain't married. Similarly, it is very difficult to lift something that doesn't exist. I lifted protective measures which were granted, but only up until the time until the witness would be called, so I lifted something that was non-existent. I meanwhile checked what the real procedural history was. Then I have a few decisions to deliver. The first one is a decision on the admission of portions of D9, D -- oh, we're still in private session. Now the whole of the world will miss the quote of Porgy and Bess. That's a pity. We'll return into open session. And I have to live with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I will deliver a decision on the admission of portions of D9, D10, D11, D13, D22, D53, D54, and D55. On the 22nd and 29th of May, 2007, the Prosecution made submissions on the admission into evidence of the items I just listed. Each of these items has been used by the Defence, but not tendered, during cross-examination of several witnesses. In its submissions, the Prosecution clarified that it does not seek admission of D10 and D11, and these exhibit numbers therefore will be vacated. The Prosecution has asked for portions of all the other items to be admitted. The Defence has objected to the admission of D9, D13, D53, and D54. It does not object to the admission of D22 and D55. According to the Prosecution, portions of D9, D13, D53, and D54 should be admitted into evidence in order to place the excerpts read to the witnesses during cross-examination "in their proper context." The Trial Chamber considers that re-examination is the proper occasion for the Prosecution to further clarify or create a context for the evidence elicited and the documents used during cross-examination. The Trial Chamber therefore denies the Prosecution's requests as far as D9, D13, D53, and D54 are concerned. These items are not admitted into evidence. Further, the Chamber finds that the transcripts making reference to D22 and D55 are sufficiently clear. There is therefore no need to have admitted into evidence the portions of these items proposed by the Prosecution and not opposed by the Defence. The Chamber therefore decides not to admit these items into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission of exhibits. I now will deliver the Chamber's decision on the exhibits tendered through witness Avramovic. At the outset, the Chamber notes that there may have been some unclarity as to the admission of the exhibits attached to the redacted 92 ter statement of this witness and its addenda. All of those documents are hereby admitted with the exception, of course, I would say, of Annex 63, the contested report of Mr. Visnjic. The Defence for Mr. Haradinaj tendered eight documents through this witness, namely, the documents marked for identification D140 through D147. Six of these are statements of other persons and two are military documents, all of which were put to Mr. Avramovic for his comments. Therefore, significant portions of these documents are already reflected in the record. The witness had no prior -- had not prior to his testimony seen the military documents that he was asked questions about, and overall, he was not in a position to confirm or deny what is contained in those documents. The statements sought to be admitted by the Defence were either taken by Defence or Prosecution investigators for the purposes of legal proceedings before this Tribunal. According to the case-law of the Tribunal, such witness statements are admissible only if they fulfil the requirements of Rule 92 bis, 92 ter, or 92 quater. The admission of those statements would have the effect of evading those Rules. We note that Prosecution annexes 7 to 11 to Mr. Avramovic's 92 ter statement, which are now Exhibits P130 through 134, are the contemporaneous statements of the detained Albanian man. Those statements were admitted, but the interviews were held by the Serbian Police for the purposes of their investigations at the time and those documents primarily shed light on the course and progress of those investigations. It is for these reasons that we decide not to admit the documents tendered by the Defence for Mr. Haradinaj into evidence. Only the portions of those documents which have been read into the record remain in the record. This concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. With the indulgence of the interpreters and the technicians and the transcriber, I have a very short decision remaining. Otherwise, it would take time tomorrow. It's not a decision, as a matter of fact, but these are the reasons for the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witness 56. The Prosecution applied for the assignment of a pseudonym and for face and voice distortion for this witness on the 17th of July, 2007. The Defence did not oppose the motion and the Chamber granted it on the 18th of July, 2007. For reference, the decision can be found on transcript page 7078. The Chamber has set out the standard for granting protective measures in numerous decisions, and there is no need to repeat it here. The witness has close relatives in Kosovo and occasionally travels there to visit them. The witness is afraid that the relatives would suffer retaliation should it become publicly known that he gave evidence in this case. Given the nature of the witness' testimony, the Chamber is satisfied that it may antagonise persons in the community where his relatives reside. The Chamber therefore found, on the 18th of July, that the requirements for granting protective measures had been met. This concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witness 56. We adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II but not until I have -- I, I'm making a mistake, Courtroom I, but not until I've given the opportunity to Mr. Emmerson to say a bit more about the timing of tomorrow and also not until I have given an opportunity, if that is possible, very briefly, to receive a response by counsel other than Mr. Emmerson on the issue of the witness to be added to the witness list and whether that witness should be cross-examined. I am talking about Witness Durrell [phoen]. We received already -- no, Mr. Guy-Smith gave an answer already. Other counsel were invited to do that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And failed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. Our position is the same as the position adopted by Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Ditto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then clear. Mr. Emmerson, how much time do you think you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: More or less an hour, I would expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Depending on Mr. Emmerson's questions, I'm anticipating about three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm anticipating no questions at all based upon the evidence given in the Prosecution's case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then including re-examination, I think that it's -- we should try to -- we should endeavour to have the witness excused not later than at the second break tomorrow morning, which would leave us the last session tomorrow morning for procedural matters. I'd like to thank the interpreters and the transcriber and the technicians for granting six additional minutes which I hope to regain tomorrow. We stand adjourned until quarter past 2.00 tomorrow, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of August, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
